title: Selvage Session Protocol — the two sealed payloads that are JSON, and the vocabulary a refused frame is reported in
description: `selvage/2`'s binary frame is an envelope of bytes, not a JSON frame, and its layout is CANONICAL.md §6.1's; what the envelope carries sealed is either opaque y-protocols bytes or one of these two objects. Valid against PROTOCOL.md §7.1: the room state the host publishes and the closing that ends the room. Neither is a session frame — neither carries `v` — and both are canonical when they follow CANONICAL.md §2, `listing` in the order §2.7 gives it, with §3's tolerance for a member the receiver does not know. Every object here tolerates a member it does not know, as every schema in this directory does. `refusalReason` is the third thing this file fixes and the only one that is not a payload: the local report a receiver answers a refused frame with, which no frame carries and which `PROTOCOL.md` §13.2 binds a client to produce.

refusalReason.title: the reason a refused frame is reported in
refusalReason.description: The receiver's local report, and the check order it is read in: CANONICAL.md §6.1's table, whole. A frame is refused for the first of these that applies to it, and PROTOCOL.md §13.2 requires a client to report the reason rather than drop a frame silently. It is a closed *value* rather than a member — no frame carries it, and a receiver tolerates a member it does not know (§3) — so this is the one place in this file where a string an implementation invents is refused. `bad_tag` is the reason a reader would expect and cannot have: the signature covers the ciphertext, so a flipped tag byte reaches a verifier as a signature failure and no conforming receiver can report a tag failure at all (CANONICAL.md §6.1; `docs/studies/peer-corpus.md` §5.4 measured it). `unauthorised_content` is the one reason here that is not a property of the envelope: an authentic frame from a peer the host committed as `viewer` carrying document content is refused by the peer rules (PROTOCOL.md §13.5).

sealedIssued.description: The host's edition of a sealed value: the room state's `issued`, and the `issued` a closing carries above every state the host has published. A count, in CANONICAL.md §2.4's form and inside its bound, because the receiver that compares it against the highest it has accepted may be a JavaScript one. It orders the two values the host signs; a frame's `counter` orders the frames one key signs, and the two are different numbers with different jobs (CANONICAL.md §6.1).

sealedRole.description: The role the host assigns to a peer in the room state: `host`, `guest`, or `viewer`, the role the host denies a peer's edits to. It is `common.json`'s `role` with one more value and a different author — that one is the claim a `selvage/1` connection makes about itself in `session.hello` (`PROTOCOL.md` §9), this one is a fact the host states and signs, and no server seats it. What a receiver does with a committed `viewer` is `PROTOCOL.md` §13.5's: it refuses document content from that peer and reports it `unauthorised_content`, while its SyncStep1 and its awareness are answered and applied.

sealedPeerKey.description: A peer's public key, and a key the host has committed for it to sign its own frames with: 32 bytes of Ed25519 in the encoding the invite URL's fragment writes one in — base64url, RFC 4648 §5, unpadded, so exactly 43 characters and no escape in a canonical JSON string (CANONICAL.md §2.3). The key itself and not its 8-byte id: an id is something a receiver derives (SHA-256 of these 32 bytes, first 8) and an id alone verifies nothing, so a state that carried one would commit nothing anyone could check.

sealedPeer.description: One peer as the host's state seats it. Nothing here is a value the server supplies: the server knows a peer's `peer_id` and its display name and neither of these.

roomState.title: the sealed room state
roomState.description: The host's whole statement about a room, published sealed under the frame key with kind 1 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). It replaces the receiver's previous state wholesale: a shorter `listing` is a smaller working tree and not a partial update.

listing.description: The host's working tree as it enumerated it: paths, carrying no content, each held to `PROTOCOL.md` §5's path rule and each a candidate rather than a promise of a readable file, exactly as a `selvage/1` grant's `paths` is. Written ascending by UTF-16 code unit (CANONICAL.md §2.7), which is the only order `selvage/2` promises.

peers.description: The roster the host seats, by `peer_id`, the host's own entry included: the key each peer signs its frames with and the role it is given. An object rather than `room.joined`'s array of the same name, because this one is looked up by `peer_id` and not listed. Two names for one value are a host's error and not a peer's: a receiver that reads one key under two names uses the entry whose `peer_id` comes first in UTF-16 code-unit order, so two conforming receivers read one state the same way (CANONICAL.md §6.1).

roomClosing.title: the sealed closing
roomClosing.description: The host's statement that a room is over, published sealed under the frame key with kind 2 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). One member is a constant and the other is what makes a replay of an old closing a drop rather than an end: a closing is ordered by `issued`, above every state the host has published.

closing.description: Constant. The kind is already what makes this a closing; the member is what a reader of the plaintext sees, and what keeps the payload an object rather than an empty one.
